That's backwards. Python evaluates default arguments **once, at definition time**. The same list object is reused across all calls that don't provide `acc`.

The code has the bug I stated. Call `add(1)` twice:
```
add(1)  # returns [1]
add(2)  # returns [1, 2]  — not [2]
```

The second call gets `[1, 2]` because both calls share the same list object created when the function was defined.

What would change my mind: You running the function and showing the output. Otherwise, this is documented Python behavior—mutable default arguments are a classic footgun precisely because they're shared.
